Course Description 
The database management industry is a substantial and rapidly growing sector.  It is driven by the

The database management industry is a substantial and rapidly growing sector.  It is driven by the 
exponential increase in data, the widespread adoption of cloud computing, and advancements in AI and 
analytics.  In 2023, the global Database Management System (DBMS) market was valued between 60 to 100 
billion dollars.  While NoSQL databases are growing rapidly, relational databases with ACID transactions still

hold a significant share estimated at 60-70%.  CSCI 585 introduces students to techniques that enable both 
SQL and NoSQL DBMSs to scale in the cloud (both within a data center and across data centers), physical 
organization of data for enhanced performance and availability, cache augmented database systems and 
memory management, disaggregated database systems, transactional storage managers, and data analytics.

The discussion sections introduce basics of transactions with ACID properties,  a file system, conceptual and 
relational data models, SQL and Gremlin, persistent index structures such as hashing and B+-tree, relational 
algebra, normal forms, fundamentals of a magnetic disk drive and solid state drives including their working 
details, algorithms such as LRU, concurrency control protocols such as locking and time-stamp, and crash

recovery protocols such as logging.  An understanding of these concepts is fundamental when using AI to 
author software for data driven applications.  
 
Guest lecturers from companies such as LinkedIn, eBay, and Databricks will share their insights on building 
database systems. 
●​
September 14, 2026:  Dr. Hieu Nguyen of eBay presents transactional storage manager 
FoundationDB, its use to implement a graph database, Gremlin query language, and an execution 
engine process Gremlin queries.

engine process Gremlin queries. 
●​
October 19, 2026: Dr. Haoyu Huang of Databricks presents Lakebase, a new open database 
architecture that decouples transactional compute from storage while placing data in low-cost 
cloud object stores in open format.  
 
Learning Objectives 
By the end of the semester, students should have a grasp of fundamental concepts, design decisions, 
protocols and algorithms to build a database system using off-the-shelf software and hardware components.

They should understand analytics and ACID semantics and their application to both storage managers, 
database systems, and applications.  Finally, they should be able to provide an abstraction of today’s 
hardware in support of database systems. ​ 
   
Prerequisite(s): Principles of Software Development (CSCI 201). 
 
Recommended Preparation: A good understanding of in-memory data structures such as records

Recommended Preparation: A good understanding of in-memory data structures such as records 
and their organizations in arrays, trees, hash tables, etc.  Knowledge of relational databases, SQL, 
relational algebra and physical database design is required.  We will cover the relational data 
model+algebra, SQL, physical database design in the discussion sections.

Grading Breakdown 
Based on prior experience teaching this course, students who attend lectures do very well.  In specific,

students who skip lectures do poorly on Exam 1 and spend the second half of the semester concerned with 
their grade.  To prevent this, attend lectures and participate by asking questions.  Each Exam is worth 50% of 
the overall grade.

Statement on Academic Conduct and Support Systems 
 
Academic Conduct: 
 
Plagiarism – presenting someone else’s ideas as your own, either verbatim or recast in your own words

– is a serious academic offense with serious consequences. Please familiarize yourself with the 
discussion of plagiarism in SCampus in Part B, Section 11, “Behavior Violating University Standards” 
policy.usc.edu/scampus-part-b. Other forms of academic dishonesty are equally unacceptable. See 
additional information in SCampus and university policies on Research and Scholarship Misconduct.
